summary: Describes the role of ICMP in the IP stack and sets guidelines for when adding new ICMP types and codes is desirable and when it is not. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: ICMP is the network's way of sending short warning notes. This sets rules for when it is a good idea to invent a new kind of note.

questions: when to add new icmp types
can icmp be used as a routing protocol
subtitle: Guidelines on when it is, and is not, a good idea to add new message types and codes to ICMP.

tldr.problem: There was concern about a lack of clarity on when new message types and codes should be added to ICMP, for both ICMPv4 and ICMPv6.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC limits future ICMP types to two broad categories: reporting forwarding plane anomalies downstream, and discovering and conveying dynamic information about nodes, networks and on-link routers and hosts. ICMP SHOULD NOT become a general-purpose routing or network management protocol.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 189) that gives designers a yardstick for new ICMP work and classifies the existing message types against it.

today: RFC 7279 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 189) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It stands as the policy statement on adding ICMP types and codes.

sections.title: Why a Policy Was Needed
sections.content:
There was concern about a lack of clarity around when new message types and codes should be added to ICMP, including ICMPv4 (RFC 792) and ICMPv6 (RFC 4443). This document lays out a policy on when, and when not, to move functionality into ICMP.

It came out of discussions among ICMP experts in the IP Diagnostics Technical Interest Group of the Operations and Management (OPS) area, and from concerns expressed by the OPS area leadership.

It does not replace RFC 2780, which covers the process for allocating values in the IANA registries. This RFC is about the policy applied in the standards process, not the allocation process.
sections.plainLanguage: People were not sure when it was okay to add new kinds of messages to ICMP. So some experts wrote down the rules of the road.

sections.title: The Acceptable Use Policy
sections.content:
Any future message types added to ICMP should be limited to two broad categories.

  • Informing a datagram's originator that a forwarding plane anomaly was encountered downstream. The originator must be able to tell from the ICMP message whether or not the datagram was discarded.
  • Discovering and conveying dynamic information about a node (other than information usually carried in routing protocols), discovering and conveying network-specific parameters, and discovering on-link routers and hosts.

Normally, ICMP SHOULD NOT be used to implement a general-purpose routing or network management protocol. It does have a role in conveying dynamic information about a network, which falls in the second category.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP may be used for two jobs: telling a sender that its mail hit a problem on the way, and asking neighbors who is nearby and what they are like. It should not be used to run the whole post office.

sections.title: Existing Message Types and Applications
sections.content:
The RFC sorts existing message types into four groups: IPv4 forwarding plane anomaly reporting, IPv4 router or host discovery, IPv6 forwarding plane anomaly reporting and IPv6 router or host discovery. For example, IPv4 types 3 (Destination Unreachable), 11 (Time Exceeded) and 12 (Parameter Problem) are anomaly reports, while types 8 (Echo) and 9 (Router Advertisement) are discovery. In IPv6, types 1 to 4 are anomaly reports (including 2, Packet Too Big), and types such as 128 (Echo Request), 133 to 136 (router and neighbor messages) and 155 (RPL Control Message) are in the discovery group. Several IPv4 types are marked Deprecated, and RFC 6918 formally deprecated some of them.

Some applications use ICMP error notifications, or deliberately create anomalous conditions to elicit ICMP messages, and turn them into feedback for the higher layer. PING, TRACEROUTE and Path MTU Discovery (PMTUD) are the examples given. These uses are acceptable because they use existing ICMP message types and do not change ICMP functionality.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC makes two piles of existing messages: problem reports and who-is-there questions. Tools like ping and traceroute are fine because they use the existing notes in a new way and do not change what the notes mean.

sections.title: Routing, RPL and Extending ICMP
sections.content:
ICMP is an integral part of the IP layer. It is not a routing protocol or a transport for routing information. The RFC lists characteristics that make it a poor choice for one: it is frequently filtered, it is not authenticated, and it is easily spoofed. Specialist hardware processing of ICMP would also disrupt the deployment of an ICMP-based routing or management protocol.

RPL, the IPv6 routing protocol for low-power and lossy networks (RFC 6550), uses ICMP as a transport. The RFC treats this as an exception that is anomalous and not a model for future types. RPL is not deployed on the general Internet and is limited to specific, contained networks. Using ICMP as a discovery protocol is adequate, but it does not extend to full routing capabilities.

For extending ICMP, multi-part messages are specified in RFC 4884, and extensions to ICMP SHOULD follow its requirements. Existing extensions include those for MPLS (RFC 4950) and for interface and next-hop identification (RFC 5837).
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP notes can be lost, forged and are often blocked, so they are a bad way to run a delivery route map. One special network type does it anyway, but that is an odd case that others should not copy.

sections.title: ICMPv4 versus ICMPv6 and ICMP's Role
sections.content:
Because ICMPv6 is used for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, deployed IPv6 routers, security gateways and firewalls normally let administrators configure how specific ICMPv6 message types are handled. Deployed IPv4 equipment is less likely to allow this. So, at the time of writing, ICMPv6 messages usually have a higher probability of travelling end-to-end than ICMPv4 messages.

ICMP was originally meant as a way for gateways or destination hosts to report error conditions to source hosts, and ICMPv6 is modeled after ICMPv4. It is also used for IP-layer functions such as diagnostics. ICMP is defined as an integral part of IP and must be implemented by every IP module. The word "control" in the name describes communication about the Internet's control functions, not control of the Internet. Even though ICMP has a redirect message that affects routing behavior on a LAN segment, it was not and is not used as a generic routing protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer version of ICMP gets through firewalls more often than the old one. Despite its name, ICMP does not steer the Internet. It only passes notes about how things are going.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is a high-level policy and presents no new security considerations. Any particular new ICMP type or code still needs special attention to its security implications.

ICMP is not a secure protocol and has no features to discover network security parameters or to report network security anomalies in the forwarding plane. It plays a part in the Photuris protocol (RFC 2521). New ICMP functionality also needs to consider how ICMP can be abused, with the Smurf IP DoS attack given as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: ICMP has no lock on it, so anyone who adds a new kind of note has to think about how bad people might misuse it.

viz.caption: THE TWO ALLOWED CATEGORIES FOR NEW ICMP TYPES

items.title: Forwarding plane anomalies
items.text: Tell a datagram's originator that something went wrong downstream, and whether the datagram was discarded.

items.title: Dynamic information and discovery
items.text: Convey node or network parameters, and discover on-link routers and hosts.

items.title: Not allowed
items.text: A general-purpose routing or network management protocol (SHOULD NOT).
